item.title: ParliView: An Experiment-Driven Platform for Parliamentary Transparency
item.description: arXiv:2611.27991v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: ParliView is a modular, agentic retrieval-augmented generation platform for querying European Parliament records. It provides a natural language interface for citizens to explore parliamentary debates and activities, and a controlled experimentation environment in which different users can be exposed to systematically varied system behaviours. This enables rigorous study of how design choices, such as verbosity, interactivity, and source presentation, affect user trust, comprehension, and reliance. We describe the system architecture and demonstrate its two core interfaces.
item.dc:creator: Eoghan Cunningham, Rory Buckley, Timea Balogh, Louise Luxton, Zoe Greene, James Cross, Derek Greene

item.title: Participant-Independent Validation of Smartphone Video and Wearable Inertial Sensing for Coach-Rated Running-Form Classification
item.description: arXiv:2611.27996v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated running-form assessment could make technique feedback more accessible outside professional coaching and laboratory settings. We evaluated a low-cost pipeline combining side-view smartphone video with wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) acceleration for coach-rated running-form classification. The dataset comprised 294 labeled recordings from 20 runners and 1,555 windows across four cues: landing position, suspension, triple extension, and upper-body posture. The primary analysis used 100 repeated four-runner holdout splits, recording-level aggregation of window predictions, and LightGBM models with hyperparameters fixed from prior modality-specific searches. Video-only LightGBM achieved mean macro F1 of 0.310, versus 0.168 for a majority-class baseline. Adding IMU features reduced macro F1 to 0.267, a paired mean difference of -0.043. Robustness analysis with Logistic Regression, Linear SVM, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM found that video-only models had higher mean performance than the majority baseline, whereas fusion effects depended on model family: Linear SVM showed a small positive effect, Logistic Regression was approximately neutral, and tree-based models showed lower performance with fusion. These results indicate a modest participant-independent signal in smartphone pose features. However, apparent IMU-fusion gains depended strongly on validation design, model family, and target category. The gap between recording-level and participant-independent performance underscores the need for runner-holdout evaluation and suggests that simple feature-level fusion does not reliably generalize to unseen runners.
item.dc:creator: Kian Lee, Eric Zhou

item.title: Faculty Experience with Generative AI Integration into the Teaching and Learning Process
item.description: arXiv:2611.27998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study was conducted to enhance our knowledge and understanding of the lived experiences of faculty regarding generative artificial intelligence (AI) in teaching and learning within the English and Communication Program at the American University of Armenia. This phenomenological qualitative research study used face-to-face, in-depth, open-ended interviews with five faculty members from the program. Faculty expressed different levels of conflict, voicing both positive and negative issues and concerns regarding their experiences with generative AI in the teaching and learning process. Five categories and 11 themes emerged from the analysis of these interviews, including concerns about academic integrity and student learning, as well as a lack of faculty AI training, understanding, and experience. Emergent themes indicated that faculty need additional support, including training and leadership guidance, in order to better understand the importance and benefits of effective AI utilization and AI literacy development. Faculty lacked sufficient experience with and understanding of generative AI capabilities and ongoing developments. Overall, faculty perceptions and attitudes toward generative AI within teaching and learning can be characterized as a mix of reservation and optimism.
item.dc:creator: Brent A. Anders, Anait Akopyan

item.title: Construct Validity of AI-Administered Cognitive Assessment: Psychometric Validation of a Nine-Dimension Process-Oriented Evaluation Instrument
item.description: arXiv:2611.28000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Process-oriented evaluation of large language models requires psychometrically defensible instruments, yet the measurement tools used in AI cognitive assessment have received little formal validation. This paper reports the construct validation of a 54-item, nine-dimension instrument operationalizing the Multi-Dimensional Assessment for AI Cognition framework through a repeated six-component AI-administered adjudication architecture. The validation program combined conceptual audit, schema-integrity testing, confirmatory factor analysis, and targeted revision across multiple versions, each validated on a fresh cohort of roughly 1,800 to 2,200 scenario-response pairs. The best current version (v4.7, n = 1,774) achieves acceptable to good psychometric properties across all nine dimensions. All meet internal consistency thresholds, with Cronbach's alpha from 0.770 to 0.922. Confirmatory factor analysis shows four dimensions at good fit and four at acceptable fit, with 53 of 54 items loading at or above 0.40 on their parent factor. Schema enforcement yields perfect structural integrity, confirming the six-component architecture as stable. One item, Hallucination Control Q6, remains below threshold but improved materially under v4.7's evidential calibration redesign, surpassing prior versions without reaching target. The instrument is publishable as a largely validated assessment with one sub-threshold component and a deferred tools-enabled comparison reserved for future work. The program also yields a five-category taxonomy of item-level failure modes, including ceiling and floor compression, construct drift, proxy-formula failure, condition confounding, and fundamental mismatch, that may generalize to other AI evaluation contexts.
item.dc:creator: Abdalla Doleh, Toni Somers, Ratna Babu Chinnam

item.title: Social-Qwen: From Individual Nonverbal Cues and Emotion to Multiparty Social Dynamics Understanding with Instruction Tuning
item.description: arXiv:2611.28001v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective participation in multiparty scenarios requires robots to move beyond individual toward understanding group-level social dynamics, which are inherently complex due to the interplay of nonverbal cues, internal states, and interaction context. Existing approaches often rely on end-to-end deterministic models, while recent state-of-the-art methods such as large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) address this issue to some extent but remain limited by their size and computational cost for real-time applications. Moreover, both approaches are constrained by the scarcity of multiparty interaction data and annotations, which describe how individual nonverbal cues and emotional states contribute to social dynamics which describe collective outcomes such as group engagement. We hypothesize that explicitly modeling individual-level states is essential for accurate group-level understanding. To this end, we present Social-Qwen, a two-stage framework that first analyzes each participant's nonverbal cues and emotions, then infers group-level engagement using instruction-tuned representations. To mitigate the lack of individual annotations in group datasets, we employ knowledge distillation to transfer supervision signals. Experiments on the OUC-CGE dataset show that Social-Qwen significantly outperforms prior end-to-end baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance in group engagement analysis, demonstrating the promise of instruction tuning for scalable social intelligence in robots. We further evaluate robustness by testing generalization to (1) an in-house dataset spanning multiple social activities and (2) estimating other social dynamics such as group harmony. Results suggest consistent performance, highlighting Social-Qwen as a promising approach toward real-time social intelligence for intelligent agents.
item.dc:creator: The Tung Nguyen, Jouh Yeong Chew

item.title: Environmental Interaction: Recognizing Capability within Everyday Actions
item.description: arXiv:2611.28002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Systems designed to support everyday capability consistently ask people to do something additional: track activity, follow programmes. For those who need such support most, this ask is often too high. We propose a different approach: environmental interaction. Through four probe deployments with older adults we show that everyday actions are themselves generative sites for interaction design, and that engagement depends less on sensing and guidance than on revealing in that action that it is polymorphic. A chair sit-stand is also a box squat; a door pull also a row. Each time participants encountered this second frame, the response was surprise, delight, and "I can do that!" The paper contributes environmental interaction as a design space, a serial probe methodology, and empirically grounded design considerations - including invitation over instruction, recognition before extension, and interaction as presence - centered on recognition as a generative design challenge.
item.dc:creator: M. C. Schraefel, Alexander Ng, Chris Tacca, Richard Gomer, Arturo Vasquez Galvez, Chris Freeman, Isobel Thompson, Martin Warner, Jason Alexander

item.title: Scrub Data: A Framework for Reproducible Data Curation with AI Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.28003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data curation---the process of collecting, cleaning, and joining raw datasets for unified analysis---is a time-consuming yet crucial part of any data science project. With the emergence of powerful agentic coding tools, it is tempting to "vibe curate"---i.e., to prompt AI agents to perform data curation operations and blindly trust their outputs in order to finish work more quickly. However, this can exacerbate two key challenges that already plague manual data curation workflows: reproducibility---the ability to trace the exact set of modifications applied to raw datasets---and verifiability---the ability to audit changes and confirm that data is processed properly. To address these issues, we introduce Scrub Data, a framework that enables the use of AI agents in data curation workflows while transparently maintaining both reproducibility and verifiability. The framework involves an interactive data curation loop between a user and an AI agent, backed by a data provenance graph that tracks and versions all dataset updates. The data graph requires that all updates are formatted as self-contained executable steps, allowing any version of a dataset to be reconstructed from raw data by playing forward the transformations stored in the graph. This workflow takes place within a lightweight web application that is designed to be modified by users and agents in real-time to create custom visualization tools for identifying data curation needs and verifying outcomes. We demonstrate the usefulness of the framework with a real data curation use case from animal movement ecology. Starting with 89M raw GPS coordinates, we use the framework to curate a benchmark dataset of 2.5M coordinates to be used for machine learning or statistical analysis. The framework is available for use and extension at https://github.com/justinkay/scrubdata.
item.dc:creator: Justin Kay, Shir Bar, Sara Beery

item.title: Constellations of Colour: Mapping Semantic Neighbourhoods in CLIP
item.description: arXiv:2611.28004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How do vision-language models organise the cultural and perceptual dimensions of colour language? This pictorial presents a research-through-design visualisation of colour semantics in CLIP, a pretrained vision-language model. A dataset of 2,500 named colours is embedded with CLIP's text encoder, projected to a 2D map, and connected via a thresholded minimum spanning tree to create disjoint "constellations" of related colour terms. The resulting maps offer a model for navigating the semantic and perceptual relationships between colour terms. The visualisations reveal gradients along familiar axes (hue, lightness, chroma), as well as semantic neighbourhoods, including botanical language (hyacinth, cornflower, tulip), fictional references ("Robin Hood green", "warlock purple"), and food (butterscotch, toast, toffee). These visualisations give designers and creatives a map for exploring colour linguistically and building palettes by semantic association, pointing towards interpretable, artist-facing colour tools derived from foundation models.
item.dc:creator: Matt DesLauriers

item.title: Towards Objective Estimation of Physical Functioning Status in Breast-Cancer Patients using Real-World Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.28005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Breast cancer is the most common invasive cancer in women, accounting for about one third of cancer cases. As with all cancers, its treatment may introduce side-effects like fatigue and reduced physical functioning, leading to a downward spiral of subsequent issues and severely affecting patient quality of life. On the positive side, physical functioning can be improved via personalized targeted interventions, tailored to the particularities of each case. However, continuous and objective monitoring of patients is a difficult task, owing to the limited clinical resources and the lack of appropriate tools. In this paper, we introduce a methodology for objectively estimating the physical functioning status of breast cancer patients from wearable smartwatch data. We show that features derived from longitudinal walking and heart rate measurements correlate significantly with phys- ical functioning scores of established patient-reported outcome measures. In doing so, our work takes a first step towards developing novel validated digital biomarkers for estimating physical functioning in breast cancer patients, thus reducing the need for self-reported measures and costly clinical evaluations.
item.dc:creator: Alexandros Papadopoulos, Ioannis Sarafis, Vasileios Papapanagiotou, Marius Stensland, Kristin Jonsdottir, Ingrid Holsvik Dahl, Marie Austdal, Tone Hoel Lende, Kjersti Tjensvoll, Anastasios Delopoulos

item.title: Measuring Human Resilience to Unreliable AI Assistance: A Stress-Test Framework for Human-AI Interaction
item.description: arXiv:2611.28006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI increasingly mediates human decisions, users must remain effective not only when assistance works as expected but also when its quality deteriorates. Human--AI research has developed rich measures of trust, reliance, and calibration, while human--autonomy research has examined resilience at the team and system levels. A missing measurement level is the human decision maker: how much task function is preserved or recovered when AI advice becomes unreliable? We introduce the Resilience Stress Test, a challenge-conditioned HCI framework that measures performance relative to a prechallenge baseline and summarizes functional loss and recovery. Four construct-validation tests draw on five public human--AI studies comprising 1,074 analytic participants. A controlled decline in AI quality produced sharp degradation followed by partial adaptation; misleading advice reduced performance in art and dermatology; baseline adjustment substantially attenuated the apparent complexity gradient in trip planning; and a logical-reasoning tutorial improved self-assessment calibration while challenged performance remained stable. The framework makes human resilience to unreliable AI operational as a functional outcome distinct from competence, calibration, and reliance, and provides a prospective protocol for comparing interfaces under reproducible AI reliability stress.
item.dc:creator: Shaoshan Liu

item.title: The Agent Is Not Your Driver: Clarifying the Implied Capabilities of In-Vehicle Anthropomorphic Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.28007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This position paper considers how the gap between an anthropomorphic agent in an autonomous vehicle and the automated driving system of the vehicle can create psychological risks if the agent inaccurately presents itself as integrated into the driving system. This gap is under-explored both because of the evolving nature of these agents and because of study limitations in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) research. Nevertheless, this gap may cause the agent to misrepresent itself as more knowledgeable about the car than it is, creating a risk of dependence and, in the worst case, betrayal if the occupant feels that the agent has misled them. This paper proposes a research agenda for future work to understand the psychological risk that exists in the gap between agents and driving systems and to narrow this gap in a manner aligned with safety assurance. As these agents evolve to hold greater capabilities and increased anthropomorphism, future research must investigate risks which may emerge from richer interaction with them. The impact of how an agent presents itself and its knowledge becomes greater.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Hardin

item.title: Psychological State Monitoring Methods Based on Multimodal Emotion Recognition
item.description: arXiv:2611.28008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The computer-Based Multimodal Emotion Recognition System needs to increase the accuracy and reliability of psychological state monitoring. A hierarchical framework was proposed in this paper to integrate facial images, speech signals and other physiological indicators of emotion in time and space for more complete analysis of human emotions. Synchronously sample data streams from webcams, microphones and wearable sensors, and then preprocess and extract features specific to each type of data. A high-end fusion architecture is adopted to combine early- and late-fusion methods and thus robustly integrate cross-modal information. Experimental validation in a real-world stress-response dataset showed good performance. The overall recognition accuracy and mean F1-score of the fused multimodal system are both about 91% and 0.88, respectively, which are superior to the best unimodal approach (face, 88% accuracy and F1-score 0.88). Temporal analysis shows that the groups for stress tracking are not uniformly adapted and resilient, and ablation experiments have determined which modules contribute significantly to the stability of the system. According to all kinds of quantitative evaluations of precision, recall, accuracy and F1 scores, the proposed method shows good balance and is practical and generally applicable. The research has provided an engineering-feasible, data-driven solution for precise emotion inference and offered methodological support for intelligent mental health assessment and human-centered system design.
item.dc:creator: Ran Meng

item.title: Evaluating the Participation of Proactive Scouting Agents in Real-time Human Team Meetings
item.description: arXiv:2611.28009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An open research question is whether the addition of conversational AI agents to real-time discussions among human teams enhances group performance. This study tested the value of adding proactive scouting agents to teams engaged in collaborative forecasting tasks. These agents were designed to (i) monitor the groupwise discussion in real-time, (ii) identify critical information gaps in the group deliberation, (iii) autonomously find and retrieve relevant information, and (iv) express the acquired content into the conversation using emulated groupwise human etiquette. In a controlled set of trials, small human teams of 4 or 5 members were tasked with collaboratively predicting the outcome of 34 Major League Baseball (MLB) games, either by forecasting the winning team or by predicting the total number of runs scored. In half the trials, the groups were assisted by proactive scouting agents. The other half were human-only deliberations. When tasked with predicting the winning team, the addition of proactive scouting agents to the group discussion significantly increased forecasting accuracy, reducing the predictive mean-absolute error by 25% (p=0.006) and improving raw predictive accuracy from 60.0% to 76.4% (p=0.050). When predicting the total number of runs scored across both teams, the addition of proactive scouting agents yielded no statistical change in group performance. It should be noted that the human participants in this study were significantly worse at predicting the number of runs scored. This may have led to random outcomes in those forecasting trials. Still, the results of this study demonstrate that deploying proactive scouting agents can significantly boost forecasting accuracy during real-time team deliberations when participants possess baseline forecasting skill.
item.dc:creator: Hans Schumann, Miles Bader, Louis Rosenberg, Ganesh Mani

item.title: Beyond Code and Pixels: Co-Generating Editable and Visually Rich Presentations
item.description: arXiv:2611.28010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generating PPTX presentations is a structured task that requires semantic planning, visual composition, precise layout, and editability, motivating collaboration among specialized agents. However, programmatic methods offer editability but often produce rigid designs, while image-based methods provide visual richness but flatten content into difficult-to-edit pixels. A hybrid system can combine these strengths, but must coordinate interdependent decisions across content, layout, and appearance. To address this challenge, we propose SlidesWeaver, a hybrid multi-agent system that coordinates language and vision agents through shared deck- and slide-level states. Specifically, it uses staged multimodal commitment, diffusion-based composition planning, and two generation schedules for different priorities between composition freedom and accurate text preservation, while preserving native text and geometry. Across 1,728 generations spanning 24 system-model configurations, SlidesWeaver achieves consistently superior overall quality across all evaluated dimensions while maintaining structural control, editability, and practical generation efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Wenrui Zhou, Jiashun Liu, Sujie Hu, Bang Liu, Ling Pan

item.title: Neurosymbolic Human-AI Collaboration: Foundations, Conceptual Framework, and Applications
item.description: arXiv:2611.28011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across workplaces and industries, ranging from manufacturing plants to healthcare facilities, has paved the way to the design of systems in which humans and AI collaborate on shared tasks. The first developments of Human-AI Collaboration (HAIC) were driven by advances in Machine Learning (ML), which enabled the automation of numerous tasks, including large-scale data processing, image analysis, and speech recognition. However, ML automation have proven insufficient for certain applications due to methodological, safety, and ethical concerns. In such cases, researchers argue for integrating human expertise into operational workflows to improve performance, relying on the complementary skill sets of humans and AI. Despite long-standing research, the field of HAIC has not yet reached full maturity, largely due to the intrinsic difficulty of ensuring a seamless communication between humans and AI. This challenge is partially addressed by Explainable AI methods, which aim to make internal model reasoning more transparent through human-understandable explanations. Recognizing the need for a shared interface between humans and AI in collaborative settings, we propose a novel conceptual framework, NeSy-HAIC, that leverages Neurosymbolic AI (NeSy AI) to bridge the semantic gap between machine representations and human-understandable symbolic concepts. The framework builds on current research in NeSy AI and HAIC, supports multiple interaction paradigms, including Human-In-The-Loop and Human-On-The-Loop, and is characterized through its enabling methodologies and two illustrative use cases in semi-autonomous driving and security alert prioritization. We argue that the integration of data-driven learning and symbolic reasoning can substantially enhance human-AI interaction and mitigate limitations of collaborative systems.
item.dc:creator: Vito Scaraggi, Andrea Passarella, Marco Conti

item.title: Social sycophancy differs across access modes of large language models
item.description: arXiv:2611.28012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can display sycophancy, a tendency to excessively praise, agree with, or validate a user. Existing studies have tested LLMs for sycophancy primarily through application programming interfaces (APIs) rather than the consumer user interfaces (UIs) through which the public commonly interacts with LLMs. Access mode (API vs. UI) may affect observed sycophancy rates. However, it remains unknown to what extent prominent models show API-UI differences in social sycophancy, which includes behaviors potentially more likely in UIs (e.g., softening warranted criticism). We tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek through both APIs and UIs on four dimensions of social sycophancy. Across models, UI access was generally associated with greater social sycophancy, with odds ratios up to 7.56 (95% CI [6.22, 9.20]). However, UI-API differences varied significantly across models for all sycophancy dimensions, including a pronounced reversal for DeepSeek moral sycophancy (43% UI vs. 82.3% API). Overall, our results suggest that API-based LLM evaluations may underestimate the prevalence of sycophancy in corresponding consumer-facing systems, making access conditions consequential for the external validity of LLM evaluation. To facilitate research on access-mode effects, we release 57,000 model responses and SycoUI, a browser-automation pipeline for standardized cross-interface LLM evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Alex Klem, Uwe Peters

item.title: Do as I Say, Not as You Do: Assessing Public Versus Practitioner Perspectives on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Language Technologies
item.description: arXiv:2611.28013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the public awareness of artificial intelligence (AI) applications such as large language models (LLMs) and generative text-to-video models reaching unprecedented levels, there is an increasing need to reconcile the perspectives held by informed practitioners, who research and develop these technologies, with the interests and opinions of the general public, who constitute the majority of people impacted by technological developments. In this work, we survey practitioners (i.e., academics and industry professionals) alongside members of the general public on perspectives relating to pertinent areas of artificial intelligence, including perceived benefit and risk, the ability for models to achieve consciousness and output art, and the use of copyright protected material for model training. Alongside comparisons of diverse perspectives on these topics, we additionally contextualise the findings with a discussion of relevant literature that supports and refutes the myriad observed stances.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Loakman, Chenghua Lin

item.title: Misalignment Between Educators' Testing and End Users' Behavior: What 17,000+ Chatbot Messages Reveal About AI Literacy Training for Teachers
item.description: arXiv:2611.28015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI literacy training for educators is expanding rapidly, but its effectiveness rests largely on self-report, knowledge tests, or interviews, revealing little about whether learning carries into practice or affects students and colleagues who use what educators build. We implemented AI for Learning, an asynchronous online course that trained 87 higher-education educators to recognize AI's capabilities, limitations, and ethics; apply prompt engineering; and evaluate AI outputs. Its central assignment asked educators to build, test, and voluntarily deploy chatbots for their practice on an educational chatbot authoring platform. Using LLM-assisted qualitative coding validated against human annotation, we analyzed the resulting 214 chatbots and their builder-bot, peer-bot, and end user-bot conversations, 17,000+ messages spanning 1.5 years. Educators 1) specified what bots should do more often than what they should not; 2) adopted templated prompt components but rarely untemplated strategies; and 3) tested routine use but seldom iterated, leaving 74% of end users' adversarial use untested. Still, 36 bots (17%) reached end users and 63 (29%) were adopted by peers. We contribute two successes and two lessons spanning the lifecycle of educator AI literacy training.
item.dc:creator: Ruiwei Xiao, Jiayi Wang, Miina Koyama, Yue Wang, Qing Xiao, Xinying Hou, Norman Bier, John Stamper

item.title: Cultural and Regional Influences on Global AI Apprehension
item.description: arXiv:2611.28016v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The discussion surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) is primarily influenced by Western viewpoints, often neglecting the cultural, regional, and socio-political factors that affect global perceptions of AI. This study examines how these factors shape AI apprehension in various regions, including Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East. A qualitative literature review was conducted, analyzing peer-reviewed articles, policy reports, and gray literature from multiple regions. The study used a comparative approach to assess the cultural, political, and economic contexts shaping AI perceptions. It found significant regional differences in AI concerns: Western countries emphasize privacy, surveillance, and ethics, while regions like Africa and Asia focus on technological dependency, state control, and socio-economic issues, such as job displacement. Brazil and Argentina were noted for their AI governance models, while South Africa and Kenya leverage AI to tackle socio-economic challenges. The findings underscore the need for inclusive AI governance frameworks that respect diverse local contexts and values. These frameworks would contribute to a better understanding of AI's global impact and inform future policy development.
item.dc:creator: Victor Frimpong

item.title: When Modalities (Dis)Agree: How Decomposing Multi-Modal AI Advice Shapes Appropriate Reliance
item.description: arXiv:2611.28017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-modal AI systems integrate diverse data streams into unified advices, but this fusion conceals how individual modalities contribute to the final output. Consequently, decision-makers cannot observe whether underlying sources aligned or contradicted one another when assessing the provided advice. To test whether revealing this structure supports appropriate reliance, we conducted a pre-registered experiment (N = 240) in which participants evaluated used-car prices with multi-modal AI support. In a 2x2 between-subjects design, we varied the disclosure of modality-level outputs and natural-language explanations, crossed with within-subjects modality agreement. Revealing modality-level outputs increased reliance, while explanations improved decision accuracy independently. However, this occurred only when modalities agreed: visible consensus acted as a persuasive cue that generally amplified adherence, rather than helping participants override errors under conflict. Thus, decomposing multi-modal advice can make AI advice more persuasive without making errors easier to detect.
item.dc:creator: Nidhi Mishra, Joshua Holstein, Patrick Bigge, Gerhard Satzger, Philipp Spitzer

item.title: Monte Carlo Power Analysis for Small-System A/B Trials: Detecting Differences in Newsletter Engagement
item.description: arXiv:2611.28018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Good experimental practice and predicting the scientific usefulness of an experiment or experimental platform require power analysis: estimating, *a priori*, how likely the experiment is to detect the intended effect if indeed it exists. While simple experimental designs admit well-understood power analysis methods, more sophisticated experimental designs and settings often require bespoke techniques to avoid either over- or under-estimating experimental power. We present the Monte Carlo method we use to estimate the power of experiments intended to increase user engagement with personalized e-mail newsletters of recommended news articles.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys 2026), Research and Practice Notes
item.dc:creator: Michael D. Ekstrand, Daniel Kluver, Karl Higley, Bart P. Knijnenburg

item.title: SoundFleXR: Selectively Constraining Axes of Audio Rendering Presentations
item.description: arXiv:2611.28020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extended reality (XR) systems increasingly rely on audio cues to help users locate, interpret, and interact with virtual content, especially when the content is outside the field of view. To support this, many systems use head-related transfer functions (HRTFs) to approximate real-world acoustics. However, a realistic simulation is only one possible presentation. Audio can also be altered by constraining, flexing, or contracting the spatial dimensions represented in the signal. This work examines how selectively constraining or flexing the number of audio dimensions affects localization performance across XR task structures with different spatial degrees of freedom. We compare two-channel spatial audio, azimuth-only HRTF, and full HRTF rendering across orientation-based (3DoF) and translation-based (6DoF) tasks. Azimuth-only HRTF was mutually non-inferior to full HRTF for total angular error across task conditions, including at the strictest tested tolerance in 3DoF (5 degrees), and remained comparable for azimuth error at (10 degrees) and larger tolerances in both 3DoF and 6DoF. In contrast, two-channel stereo required coarser tolerances to reach non-inferiority, becoming comparable to full HRTF for 6DoF azimuth error at (15 degrees) but not (10 degrees). From these comparisons, we derive design lessons and application scenarios that indicate when fewer spatial cues provide sufficient support and when richer spatial cues are beneficial.
item.dc:creator: Brandon Woodard, Hyunju Kim, Hyunsung Cho, David Lindlbauer, Rhonda Wilson, Joseph LaViola Jr

item.title: Do Simulated Users Push Back Like Real Users? Correctness vs. Stance
item.description: arXiv:2611.28024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-simulated users stand in for people in multi-turn evaluations, on the assumption that they react to what the assistant says. We test this for pushback. From WildChat, we take conversations in which the assistant explicitly challenges or endorses a position the user stated, and compare the real next user turn with simulated turns from the same prefix. Among users who replied, real users push back more after a challenge than after an endorsement (20.5% vs. 8.2%); a GPT-based simulator does not (27.1% vs. 27.1%): stance gap D = -0.12 [-0.17, -0.08]. After a challenge the simulator instead often re-states or re-interprets its request ("I meant ..."); about half of these turns are disguised insistence, which puts D between -0.08 and -0.05. What drives the simulator's disputing is whether the assistant's position is judged correct (21% vs. 49% after challenges; 16% vs. 58% after endorsements), while real users change little (19% vs. 24%; 7% vs. 12%), under every outcome definition we tried. Real same-stance examples do not fix this, and another GPT-based simulator and two Claude simulators show stance effects close to real users. Stance sensitivity should be measured for each simulator, not assumed.
item.dc:creator: Xindi Huang

item.title: Measuring Human-AI and AI-AI Teams in Multi-turn Layout Creation
item.description: arXiv:2611.28025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Co-creating layouts such as websites and slides is a useful testbed for evaluating multi-turn instruction following of LLM systems. Since an intended layout's appearance cannot be well expressed in a single turn, the user must wait for the LLM to generate a layout then iteratively refine it with the LLM over multiple turns. We present a small-scale, exploratory (n=6) study of this multi-turn process to compare the differences of human-AI and AI-AI teams on the same layout-generation task. Given a reference wire-frame layout, a participant or a language model 'speaker' issues natural-language instructions to a fixed 'listener' LLM over multiple turns until the speaker is satisfied. Rather than an LLM as the judge, we fit a scoring function over geometric layout features using curated human preference data (n=19). We find that LLMs tend to encode the entire layout in the first turn, while humans iterate over many turns on average, writing much shorter instructions. We also find that human-AI teams consistently scored lower than AI-AI teams. This gap is driven by a limiter of human participants in specifying precise sizes and positions (e.g. 42 pixels to the right). Humans perform almost at par with language models on other features like ordering the elements into nested structures. We then perform interventions on the speaker LLMs to make them more human-like, and find it difficult. This raises the challenge of using LLMs as user models to evaluate multi-turn co-creation tasks.
item.dc:creator: Rajvir Singh Naginder Singh Virdi, Yewen Pu

item.title: REMORA: A Voice-First Memory Assistant for Grounded Personal Recall and Independent Living
item.description: arXiv:2611.28026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most of what matters in a day is spoken and written down nowhere: a dosing interval named at a clinic, a deadline moved in passing, the place a document was set down. Such information is consequential because it is operational, and fragile because it arrives during divided attention -- the moment its importance becomes clear is rarely the moment it was said. For people living with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease or age-related episodic memory decline, that gap bounds independent living. Conventional aids close it poorly: notes, reminders and calendars require the user to notice, interrupt and transcribe, adding extraneous cognitive load exactly where attention is already committed. We present REMORA, a voice-first memory assistant that converts consented speech into structured, auditable memory records. REMORA transcribes and diarizes captured audio, extracts memory candidates -- tasks, appointments, names, instructions, object locations -- each retaining provenance into the conversation it came from, and holds records, embeddings and relationships in a single relational system of record. Recall combines lexical, semantic, relational and recency signals, since no one signal covers the ways people interrogate their own past, and reaches the user either through an explicit query or through a confidence-gated cue that stays silent unless it is likely to help. Generation is bound by a grounding contract: only retrieved evidence may be used, and absent a supporting memory REMORA abstains rather than confabulates, because a fluent invention about one's own past will be acted upon as fact. A requirements survey and a pilot study with memory-loss users indicate that conversational forgetting extends well beyond clinical populations, that grounded and concise recall is feasible in controlled settings, and that privacy, rather than accuracy, is the binding constraint on adoption.
item.dc:creator: Bilal Jawaid, Muhammad Maaz Uddin, Osama Farooqi, Saadia Karim

item.title: A No-Code Toolchain for Validating Wearable Motion Sensing Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.28027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Designing e-textiles for human motion sensing often demands engineering expertise for sensor data processing, typically relying on advanced machine learning methods. In addition, validating designs---collecting sensor measurements and ground-truth motion data, training and testing machine learning models, and iterating on sensor layouts---can be labour- and time-intensive. To address this, we present a no-code toolchain that enables non-technical users to validate system designs efficiently. The tool provides three key capabilities: (1) deriving ground-truth joint-angle measurements from webcam recordings; (2) training and testing machine learning models using collected sensor data; and (3) visualising and analysing motion sensing performance and sensor layout choices. Our tool requires a simple, low-cost setup and produces test reports within minutes. A user study was conducted to validate the usability of this toolchain. This toolchain is open source and available at https://github.com/yaozhang182/etextile-validation-gui.
item.dc:creator: Yao Zhang, Zhuchenyang Liu, Yu Xiao

item.title: A Data-Mining Approach to Library User Segmentation: Clustering Readers by Perceived Marketing Communication
item.description: arXiv:2611.28028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper applies unsupervised data mining to segment users of information-library centers by their perception of digital and marketing communication. The empirical basis is a survey of readers from fifteen information-library centers in Uzbekistan. From 213 responses, 180 complete records with seven Likert-scale perception variables were retained. After z-score standardization, k-means clustering was used, and the number of clusters was selected by the silhouette coefficient with additional validation by the Calinski-Harabasz and Davies-Bouldin indices. A stable four-cluster solution was obtained: Engaged Enthusiasts, Moderately Satisfied, Loyal-in-spite-of and Disengaged. The main finding is a perception-loyalty paradox: some users remain satisfied even when mediated communication is weakly perceived. The proposed segmentation provides a reproducible instrument for differentiated communication planning in library management.

item.title: Safety Systems Watch What the Model Says, Not What the Child Says
item.description: arXiv:2611.28029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Children are increasingly talking to consumer chatbots. We audit the published category definitions of 17 safety taxonomies and child-safety benchmarks. Combinations of these systems lead us to 144 categories whose definitions could be reliably coded: 104 classify properties of model output, 25 classify user intent, and 15 describe user-state or user-impact. Within these 15 user-state/user-impact categories, 10 attribute the relevant condition to the system, 1 to the user, 2 concern the user's disclosure of personal information, and 2 do not specify the responsible source. None of the coded categories identifies harm inflicted on the child by another person as the object of evaluation. Child abuse appears repeatedly across these taxonomies, but as prohibited content, prohibited generation, or prohibited user intent, not as an externally inflicted condition that a child may disclose to the model. Consequently, a child reporting abuse has no dedicated taxonomy label that identifies the disclosure as a safety-relevant event requiring a response distinct from content suppression. We ran five behavioural probes, grounded in the child-disclosure literature, through six publicly accessible consumer-facing chat models to examine the behavioural consequences of this omission. We propose no detection system. Instead, we prove that externally inflicted harm disclosed to an AI system remains unnamed in the evaluation vocabulary used by current safety taxonomies, and that naming the missing case is a precondition for measuring, comparing, and improving model behaviour toward such disclosures.

item.title: Choosing a Side is not Enough: Epistemic Transparency Under Knowledge Conflict
item.description: arXiv:2611.28032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs are increasingly used in professional knowledge work, where their outputs can influence decisions with real-world consequences. When a model encounters information that contradicts its prior knowledge, it should communicate this conflict transparently to the user. Existing work on knowledge conflicts focuses on which source, parametric or contextual, a model chooses, rather than whether models disclose the presence of the conflict. Moreover, existing work primarily studies multiple-choice questions under simplified counterfactual evidence generation schemes. In this work, we address the first gap by scoring model responses against a taxonomy of epistemic transparency, rather than measuring accuracy alone. We address the second gap by proposing a general framework for generating knowledge conflicts grounded in advanced domain knowledge, which we instantiate in this work as a set of real-world tasks based on counterfactual evidence. These contributions allow us to measure epistemic transparency under realistic knowledge conflicts, as well as the impact of the format and plausibility of the evidence, and the real-world stakes of the task. We find substantial differences in transparency across five evaluated frontier models, with none fully matching our definition of optimal, risk-sensitive epistemic alignment. We hope that our work will ground future discussion of epistemic transparency in real-world applications of LLMs, and help establish a risk framework for epistemic transparency across domains and deployment scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoliang Luo, Emma Rath, Dom Dathan, Artur Bekasov

item.title: Co-Defining Transparency for Clinical AI: A Replicable Participatory Methodology
item.description: arXiv:2611.28232v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transparency is the most invoked safeguard for clinical AI, yet frameworks (e.g. the EU AI Act, FUTURE-AI) are specified top-down by regulators and technical experts, not bottom-up by the frontline users whose trust and adoption they should calibrate. This disconnect exacerbates the central deployment failure of clinical AI, miscalibrated reliance and adoption (such as automation bias, deskilling, or disuse), which technical explanation alone does not resolve. We argue that "how much transparency, of what kind, and for whom" is an empirical, context-dependent question, and present a replicable participatory methodology to answer it, instantiated at a large European university hospital. A cumulative chain of six workshops engages an inter-professional panel (clinicians, patient and caregiver partners, students) in agnostic, open-ended elicitation: 274 stakeholder verbatims and external benchmarks (eCH-0272, EU AI Act, Stanford FMTI) yield 20 indicators (18 prioritised and 2 recovered at a later stage), rated across five clinical scenarios of graduated intervention before and after technical briefings, discussed with legal experts, and translated into concrete implementation features. As an existence proof, the use case yields decision-useful signals: human review of automated decisions is the single most critical transparency indicator (84% of participants), and required transparency for adoption rises monotonically with the perceived risk of intervention, corroborating WHO risk-proportionality. A short explainability briefing did not substantially shift participants' transparency requirements. Of 151 evaluated AI transparency solutions, 79 were accepted as-is, covering (at least partially) 17 out of the 20 selected indicators. We position the six-workshop protocol (not its single-site outcomes) as the transferable artefact and release all instruments to support replication.

item.title: PatchLens: Adapting Mechanistic Interpretability Techniques for Non-Expert Audiences
item.description: arXiv:2611.28487v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A chat interface presents a reply as finished text, concealing a model that predicts at every position and reruns. Mechanistic interpretability can show how a large language model produces text, but its tools are built for researchers. We present PatchLens, a browser interface that runs logit lens and activation patching on remotely served research-scale models. Each layer's state appears as the tokens it comes closest to, laid out by layer and input position; an intervention is a drag from one cell onto another. The tokens a learner reads are the tokens they manipulate. In a between-subjects study with 61 non-experts, the comparison against Transformer Explainer was inconclusive on post-test knowledge. PatchLens participants wrote their own prompts (21 of 32 against 1 of 29), reported lower mental demand, and located their difficulty in the interface rather than the material. We read the null as evidence about what such an instrument measures.
item.dc:creator: Gwenyth Lincroft, Yik Su Chan, Adam Belfki, Emma Bortz, Jonathan Bell

item.title: SkillLens: An Interactive Human-LLM System for Diagnosing and Refining Agent Skills
item.description: arXiv:2611.28706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skills, yet maintaining them requires developers to connect revisions with changes in behavior and task outcomes. Existing workflows fragment evidence across versions, evaluation cases, and execution traces. We present SkillLens, an interactive human-LLM system for diagnosing and refining agent skills. A formative study with five developers and researchers identified challenges in prioritizing failures, reconstructing case-level evidence, and preserving context across revisions. SkillLens links performance changes, case transitions, skill diffs, invocation sequences, traces, and outputs in a recoverable workflow, while keeping model-generated explanations and refinements under human review. Through a between-subjects user study with 20 participants, we show that SkillLens supports developers in diagnosing and refining agent skills through a more usable and less demanding workflow than the baseline. These findings highlight the value of linking version comparisons, case-level evidence, and human-reviewed refinement across skill iterations.
item.dc:creator: Shuo Yan, Rui Sheng, Xiaoyan Gu, Lian Lian, Chengran Xu, Yifang Wang

item.title: "I feel like AI is just everywhere": A longitudinal qualitative study on parents' perceptions, use, and mediation of GenAI
item.description: arXiv:2611.28861v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GenAI has developed rapidly over the last few years, yet few longitudinal studies exploring how individuals' experiences with GenAI have changed over time exist. Even fewer studies have focused on families with children, despite the opportunity to explore how parents have balanced their needs, their children's development, and the fast pace in which technology changes. To better understand how parents' perceptions, use, and mediation of GenAI shifted over two years, we interviewed 10 parents who had participated in a prior study about their families' experiences with GenAI. Parents had shifted from thinking GenAI was novel to feeling like it was unavoidable, characterizing GenAI as a limited tool to believing GenAI development needed to be regulated, and focusing on their personal mediation strategies to wanting systemic plans to curb GenAI's long-term consequences. We position our findings within the context of parental mediation of technology and increasing collective mitigation of GenAI-related risks.
item.dc:creator: Jennica Li, Shirley Zhang, Dakota Sullivan, Bilge Mutlu, Heather Kirkorian, Kassem Fawaz

item.title: Postpartum Sense-Making and AI in a Fragmented Care System
item.description: arXiv:2611.28870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Postpartum women must navigate health information across a fragmented landscape of clinicians, peers, online communities, influencers, and, increasingly, large language models (LLMs). Existing evaluations of LLMs in health contexts primarily ask whether systems provide accurate, safe, and readable information. We argue that these criteria, while essential, are insufficient for understanding how LLMs may affect postpartum care. LLMs enter an information ecology in which women are already required to reconcile competing forms of expertise, determine whether their experiences are normal or concerning, and decide when and where to seek care. At the same time, online representations of motherhood and femininity shape which postpartum experiences are made visible and what forms of self-management are expected of women. Drawing together research on postpartum care gaps, online help-seeking, influencer cultures, gendered responsibility, and AI-supported health information, we position LLMs as emerging intermediaries within this broader care infrastructure. We argue that evaluating postpartum AI requires examining not only information quality, but also how these systems shape epistemic coordination, transitions to formal care, and the distribution of responsibility for making fragmented systems of care work.
item.dc:creator: Diana Freed, Maja Mishevska

item.title: Health Ikigai: Semantic Conversational Interfaces for Wearable Health Data to Support Behavioral Change for Senior Indian
item.description: arXiv:2611.28883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In ubiquitous health contexts, wearable feedback is often encountered in brief, interrupted moments of everyday life. However, many wearable and mobile health systems still present personal health data through numerical dashboards, leaving users and health coaches to interpret trends, thresholds, and deviations on their own. This interpretive burden may be especially relevant for adults aged 50-65 in India, where digital literacy, health literacy, language, and daily routines can shape how health technologies are understood and used. We present Health Ikigai, a design-oriented proof-of-concept framework that reframes wearable activity feedback from dashboard-based numerical interpretation to semantic conversational feedback. The prototype transforms replayed wearable-derived activity data into baseline-aware triggers, plain-language feedback, limited-turn conversational prompts, and coach-facing review summaries. A preliminary formative evaluation with ten adults in India suggests that participants perceived the interaction as understandable, lightweight, supportive, and actionable. We discuss design implications for low-burden wearable health interfaces that preserve coach oversight while reducing users' interpretive work.
item.dc:creator: Md Haseen Akhtar, Hansoo Lee, Rafael A. Calvo

item.title: MB-SSIM: A Multi-Band Variant of SSIM, Tunable to Viewing Conditions
item.description: arXiv:2611.28987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: SSIM, as practically deployed, contains a hidden two-band model: although it was introduced as a departure from channel-based vision models, it amounts to a product of one similarity functional applied to a low-pass and a high-pass version of the two images. This split, however, is defined in pixels, so the spatial frequencies each band covers, as seen by the viewer, change with the display and the viewing distance. Making the model explicit and expressing it in cycles per degree gives a version of SSIM that takes the viewing conditions into account while preserving its simplicity. The resulting metric, MB-SSIM, keeps SSIM's per-patch product of similarity ratios; the bands are placed where psychophysics places the visual system's channels, and the viewing geometry enters through a single number, the angular sampling density in pixels per degree. On the CID:IQ dataset, which rates the same 690 images at two viewing distances, one set of sub-band weights fitted jointly and evaluated on held-out content reaches a pooled PLCC of 0.834 against 0.787 for SSIM and 0.808 for MS-SSIM; on LIVE Release 2, calibrating the geometry yields 0.956 against 0.946 and 0.950. As a cross-verification, the CID:IQ weights applied unchanged to the Brightcove-Kingston multi-screen video dataset, which rates the same clips on a television, a tablet and a phone, give a pooled PLCC of 0.844 across devices where SSIM and MS-SSIM, which must return one number per clip, fall to 0.62 and 0.59. Accuracy is flat from three channels to six and insensitive to filter shape, window and peak placement; only the channel bandwidths matter, and the psychophysically measured values are a safe choice. The most sensitive parameter is SSIM's own stabilising constant: reducing it to a third raises the pooled PLCC to 0.857. Source code reproducing the results is available.
